clue.text: Possibly a piece of writing that offers a vague opinion?

definitions.meaning: the word 'a' is one example of the grammatical item used for unspecified nouns, hence 'possibly'

definitions.text: piece of writing that offers a vague opinion?
definitions.meaning: read whimsically, a newspaper piece whose views are unclear and noncommittal

explanation.surface: A wry dig at a columnist whose essay never commits to a firm view.
explanation.walkthrough: The grammar term is read two ways: the word 'a' is its classic instance, and a vague essay is literally an unclear written piece.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar 'a' and 'an' are the standard examples of this determiner; literally, an unclear essay is a woolly written piece.

clue.text: More than one trouble-maker is besieging politician

indicators.note: besieging means surrounding, so the word 'is' wraps around the politician

parts.note: MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A gang of agitators is laying siege to an elected representative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' does double duty only in appearance: it supplies its own letters and 'besieging' tells them to surround MP.
explanation.definitionFit: Mischievous little devils or naughty children are plural troublemakers, a common synonym.

clue.text: Girl trapped shortly in eating area

parts.note: Di is a girl's name, short for Diana

indicators.note: shortly means the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: trapped, as with a net, is netted

explanation.surface: A young woman finds herself briefly stuck in a dining spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' looks like it means 'soon' but tells you to drop the last letter of NETTED.
explanation.definitionFit: A small room or alcove set aside for meals is a common name for a compact dining space.

clue.text: Imitating action of a card player?

definitions.meaning: copying what others have done, an idiom for conforming
in trick-taking games a player must play a card of the led kind when able

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for copying someone comes from card games, where players must match the kind of card led.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means doing as others do; literally a card player plays the same kind of card as led.

clue.text: The country's reasonable, wanting a new leader

indicators.note: the first letter is swapped for N, the abbreviation of new, giving the word a fresh head

parts.note: reasonable means rational, sensible

explanation.surface: A political remark: the state is sensible but needs someone new in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' means first letter here, not a head of government; N stands for 'new'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something belonging to a whole nation, as in national debt, is the possessive sense of 'country's'.

clue.text: Marrying and attempting not to have rows initially

indicators.note: the attempt is made without something, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: attempting is trying

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of rows

explanation.surface: A couple getting married and trying hard not to argue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rows' suggests quarrels in the surface, but only its first letter, R, matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Joining in wedlock is tying the knot, so the verb form fits marrying.

clue.text: Quiet road? The reverse — it's noisy

indicators.note: the reverse tells you to read quiet-then-road backwards

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet
a way is a road

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a quiet road is anything but, the reverse in fact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The reverse' reads like 'the opposite is true' but is the instruction to turn PWAY round.
explanation.definitionFit: A harsh raucous cry or squawk, as in Whitman's barbaric version, is certainly a noisy thing.

clue.text: Non-believer witnessing robbery

parts.note: being present at an event, as in 'at the scene'
a heist is a robbery

explanation.surface: An unbeliever happens to see a robbery take place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'witnessing' supplies AT because to be at something is to be there to see it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who denies the existence of God is the standard term for a person without religious faith.

clue.text: One with several partners, mostly a pig misbehaving

indicators.note: misbehaving letters are out of order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone with many spouses is described as largely a badly behaved pig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' looks like an instruction to shorten, but it is part of the anagram fodder MOSTLYAPIG.
explanation.definitionFit: A person married to more than one spouse at once has several partners.

clue.text: Criticise the Spanish group making decision?

parts.note: to pan a show is to criticise it harshly
el is the Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Attacking the decision of a Spanish committee.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is an example: a jury or board of judges deciding something.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of judges or experts convened to adjudicate is a board of this kind.

clue.text: Victory's strange ritual with speed being limited

indicators.note: speed is hemmed in by the rearranged letters, enclosed as a limit
strange signals letters in an odd order

parts.note: mph, miles per hour, is a measure of speed

explanation.surface: A victory celebration with an odd ceremony and a speed limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' makes TRIUAL; 'being limited' reads as a speed limit in the surface, but means the speed is enclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to or celebrating a win, as in a triumphal arch, matches the possessive 'victory's'.

clue.text: A slim young man surprisingly showing generosity

indicators.note: surprisingly suggests an unexpected arrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: A thin youth turns out, unexpectedly, to be generous.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting in a big-hearted, forgiving way is behaving generously, an adverbial synonym.

clue.text: Complete departure, terribly hot and bumpy at the outset

indicators.note: terribly suggests the letters are badly jumbled

parts.note: a ride that is bumpy from the start is rough
going is leaving, departure

explanation.surface: A total exit, on a journey hot and rough from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' makes THO; 'Complete departure' reads as one phrase, but only 'Complete' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorough and uncompromising, as in a sweeping reform, means complete or utter.

clue.text: A small herd, having gone astray, getting gathered together

indicators.note: a herd that has gone astray is scattered, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A few cattle wander off and are then rounded up.
explanation.definitionFit: To assemble troops or facts in order is the verb; gathered together is its past form.

clue.text: Idle maybe when entertained by a fellow in the USA

indicators.note: being entertained by someone, as a guest, puts you inside their place

parts.note: a fellow is a man
Eric Idle, the Monty Python comedian, so Idle is an example of someone called Eric

explanation.surface: A lazy person is hosted by a chap in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Idle' is capitalised to hide the surname of comedian Eric Idle of Monty Python; it is not about laziness.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything belonging to or found in the United States is described with this national adjective.

clue.text: Little message prohibiting Scottish headwear

parts.note: a ban is an order prohibiting something
a tam, or tam-o'-shanter, is a Scottish woollen cap

explanation.surface: A short notice forbidding the wearing of Scottish caps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little' looks like a description of the message but is the definition, as in a bantamweight or bantam hen.
explanation.definitionFit: Bantam hens and bantamweight boxers are small versions, so the word is used to mean diminutive.

clue.text: End up with girl getting covered in powder

indicators.note: the girl is wrapped by the other letters, covered on both sides
in a down clue, up means the word is written bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal
Agnes is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl ends up covered head to foot in powder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End up' looks like a phrasal verb, but in this down clue it gives a goal written upwards, MIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnesium oxide is a white powder used as an antacid and in gymnasts' chalk.

clue.text: Language in the borders of Surrey full of jargon?

indicators.note: the abbreviation sits inside the outer letters
the borders of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: lang is a standard abbreviation of language

explanation.surface: The way people talk near the edges of a Home County is full of slang. Surrey is a county south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Speech heavy with informal or insider vocabulary is described as colloquial; jargon is close kin.

clue.text: See 1
Novel set in foreign city areas with churches

indicators.note: a novel set in a city is placed inside it, so the letters go within

parts.note: Paris, a city abroad from a British view
She is the novel by H. Rider Haggard

explanation.surface: A book whose action takes place in an overseas city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' is capitalised to look like an adjective but names Haggard's She; 'set in' is both the literary phrase and the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecclesiastical districts, each with its own church and priest, are the local units of the Church.

clue.text: The male boss at newspaper with terrible flu taking care

parts.note: he is the male pronoun
ed, short for editor, runs a newspaper

indicators.note: terrible suggests the letters are in a terrible mess

explanation.surface: A male newspaper editor laid up with a nasty bout of flu, looking after himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Being attentive and mindful, paying attention to warnings, is the same as being careful.

clue.text: Author errs — man ill-suited to be an author

indicators.note: letters ill-suited to their places are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A writer makes mistakes, a man badly cut out to be a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram uses AUTHORERRSMAN; the definition is the author of the children's classic Swallows and Amazons.
explanation.definitionFit: The English writer of Swallows and Amazons is a well-known children's novelist.

clue.text: River — little one under which darling almost drowns

indicators.note: in a down clue the darling comes below the R

parts.note: a little river, i.e. its abbreviation, R

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is missing

parts.note: honey is a term for a darling

explanation.surface: A sweetheart nearly drowns beneath a small river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little one' refers back to River: its abbreviation R. HONEY, 'almost', loses its last letter and sits under R, the darling drowning beneath the river.
explanation.definitionFit: A major river flowing from Switzerland through Lyon to the Mediterranean in France.

clue.text: A positive response? More than one!

definitions.text: A positive response? More than one!

parts.words: A positive response? More than one!
parts.note: first an affirmative reply, then a call for several of them, as in a counted vote

explanation.walkthrough: The first half points to a single affirmative; the exclamation asks for several, as in a parliamentary division.
explanation.definitionFit: Votes in favour in a parliamentary division are counted with the plural of the old affirmative word.

clue.text: See small particles in positions

parts.note: lo, as in lo and behold, means see
cations are positively charged ions, tiny particles

explanation.surface: A physicist spots tiny particles in particular places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is the old exclamation lo, not a verb of seeing.
explanation.definitionFit: Places or sites where things are situated are their positions.

clue.text: Silly person dipping paper into sauce

indicators.note: dipping something into a liquid puts it inside, so the paper goes within the sauce

parts.note: soy is a sauce
FT is the Financial Times newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone foolish dunks a newspaper in soy sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paper' is a newspaper, the Financial Times, abbreviated FT.
explanation.definitionFit: A weak or soft-hearted person, a sentimental fool, is informally a softy.

clue.text: Proper learner in fight

parts.note: due means proper, as in due care
L is the learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A trainee takes part in a correct bout of combat.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal combat between two people, as with pistols at dawn, is a fight.

clue.text: Huge bikes in engineering units

parts.note: mega means huge
cycles are bikes

explanation.surface: Enormous bicycles found among engineering departments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'units' suggests departments of a firm but means units of measurement: a million cycles per second.
explanation.definitionFit: An old measure of radio frequency equal to a million oscillations per second, now the megahertz.
